postgres: PostgreSQL 17.11 on x86_64-pc-linux-musl, compiled by gcc (Alpine 15.2.0) 15.2.0, 64-bit

proofs.name: Blueprint scenarios run against the real engine
proofs.claim: Every scenario each blueprint declares, executed by the runtime that would run it in production.
proofs.detail: 22/22 scenarios passed across 3 processes.

proofs.name: Authorization is enforced by the runtime, not by the caller
proofs.claim: Section 6.1 IAM-03: every authorization check is enforced server-side. Section 12.1: deny by default.
proofs.detail: Refused: a manager from another tenant ("principal belongs to a different tenant"), an operator without the capability ("no role held (it_operator) has the "approve" capability"), a manager the request does not name ("actor is not named as an approver on this request"), and a respondent ("a respondent may not approve"). Payroll fields came back redacted to the hiring manager while the job title did not. An edit outside the role's editable fields was refused. The named approver was allowed. 5 refusals are on the audit record.

proofs.name: A form can be filled in, saved, submitted, and amended when asked
proofs.claim: Section 21 P0: value cannot exist without trustworthy intake. Section 20.1 steps 4 and 6.
proofs.detail: The published form served no classifications, roles or workflow. A hidden section appeared only once its condition was met. A half-finished draft reopened with its answers and created 0 records, because a draft is not a case. An incomplete submission was refused with 14 named fields; a complete one started a process and returned a resume link, and the draft could not be used again. Asked for changes ("Your phone number has a digit missing."), the respondent updated their phone number and was refused their bank account ("bank_account") — which the blueprint declares and nothing until now enforced.

proofs.name: Documents are real files, and email actually leaves
proofs.claim: Section 6.6: generated output stored with its checksum; a delivery log that distinguishes sent from failed.
proofs.detail: The packet is a 2633-byte PDF checksummed over its own bytes, carrying the employee's name and none of their payroll or identification data — the mapping never named those, and the renderer cannot widen it. Replaying every action produced 1 document and 1 welcome email, with the packet attached. Each send carried a distinct idempotency key, which is the same key the ledger uses, so a retry that reaches the provider is deduplicated there too. A permanent rejection was recorded as failed with its reason ("550 rejected") rather than logged as delivered.

proofs.name: A resume link opens one record and no others
proofs.claim: Section 12.3: broken object authorization in public resume and file links.
proofs.detail: The holder read their own record and was refused somebody else's ("resume token is for a different record"). A respondent with no token was refused even their own ("respondent has no resume token for any record"), and approving was refused ("a respondent may not approve"). Revoking the link made it resolve to nothing. Before this, "a respondent may view" meant any record in the tenant.

proofs.name: A draft opens, refuses to publish while broken, and says what a publish would change
proofs.claim: BLD-03, BLD-04, BLD-07 and §9.2: the compiler is the gate, and versioning is opt-in per record.
proofs.detail: Opening twice returned one draft, not two. An operator was refused ("actor holds no role in this process, and workspace role "operator" does not grant "administer""). Naming a role without the approve capability produced 2 SEC009 error(s), and publishing anyway was refused server-side ("the draft has 2 error(s) and cannot be published — SEC009: Approval "manager_app"). A draft saved as {"half":"typed"} was kept and reopened as 11 shape diagnostic(s) rather than throwing. After the fix the impact summary counted 1 record still running and named "proof_note" as added; version 2 published and the running record stayed on v1.

proofs.name: Two people editing one draft are told about each other, and neither overwrites the other
proofs.claim: Draft locking: a revision on every save and publish, and an editing lease that says who has it. A read-only member is refused on every draft route.
proofs.detail: Sam opening Joy's draft was told "Joy Builder" had it, and his save was refused (conflict:held:Joy Builder). He took over from Joy Builder; her next save was refused (conflict:held:Sam Builder), and his save from a copy older than hers was refused as stale (conflict:stale:Joy Builder). Reloaded, it landed at revision 2. Publishing an older revision: conflict:stale:you. Discarding under someone else's lease: conflict:held:Sam Builder. A read-only member on load, save, claim and publish: refused, refused, refused, refused. Published as v2; a save afterwards: conflict:published:. Releasing someone else's lease: false.

proofs.name: A script's submission is held, sends nothing, and a person is never the one who loses
proofs.claim: Spam control on public forms: a signed ticket and a trap field, and a held queue instead of a silent discard.
proofs.detail: A person with a ticket issued 95s earlier went straight through. Four scripts were held for no_ticket, too_fast, bad_ticket, trap_filled; between them they made 0 records and queued 0 actions, so the address they each named as manager was sent nothing. The real owner of an address a script had used submitted afterwards and got their own record rather than being folded into the script's. An operator saw 4 held; a read-only member saw 0 and was refused when releasing. Releasing one made a record under the held id and queued 1 action(s); releasing it again returned the same record. Releasing the one that shared an address joined the existing record (duplicate: true). Discarding cleared every answer, and a release afterwards was refused.

proofs.name: The bounce rate is watched, and an address that comes back gets what it missed
proofs.claim: Bounce-rate alerting against the provider's review thresholds, and re-sending after a suppression is lifted.
proofs.detail: 61 messages went out. With none bouncing the check was silent; at 2 hard bounces (3.3%) it raised a watch alert, and asking again a moment later raised nothing. At 5 (8.2%) it escalated to act, and a week later, with the bounces out of the window, it cleared — 3 emails to the ops address in all: "Watch: bounce or complaint rate is rising", "Act now: bounce or complaint rate is at the provider’s review threshold", "Sending has recovered". This workspace's share counted 5 bounces; a quiet workspace's counted 0 sent. A message to a suppressed address was recorded as missed (1), a resend while it was still suppressed was refused, and after reinstating it the resend went once — to that address, under key resend:61:person41@proof-health.test — and a second press sent nothing ("already sent again").

proofs.name: Many records at once: previewed per record, confirmed as a set, and reported
proofs.claim: §6.4 bulk actions — assignment and status change — through the same preview, digest and per-record checks as reminders.
proofs.detail: Reassigning equipment to it2 previewed 2 records (from role:it_operator) and skipped 1 with no open task. An operator previewing the same was refused on 2 — reassignment is an administrator's call. A deactivated member was refused ("leaver@proof-bulk.test has been deactivated") and so was a member with no role on the process. Confirming as somebody else was refused; a stale digest was refused; confirming ran 2 and a second confirm was refused. The old assignee could no longer complete the task (refused); the new one did. Withdrawing three records moved the two in manager review and skipped the one in provisioning ("nothing in the process moves a record from Setting up equipment and accounts to Withdrawn by hand"); an IT operator was refused ("only HR administrator may move it from With hiring manager to Withdrawn"); a move into provisioning did not compile (ACT007), because nothing moves a record there by hand. The two withdrawn records each got the withdrawal notice the step sends — 2 in all.

proofs.name: Two workspaces with the same process each get their own form and their own records
proofs.claim: Public form links name one workspace’s form; the old key-only link refuses once it is shared; the public API is scoped to its key’s workspace.
proofs.detail: Workspace A published once and B twice, which is the case that used to hand A's applicants to B. A's link (x7f7-4y3y-n2hy) served A's form at version 1; B's (ap4w-qdk5-mmxh) served B's. A submission through each landed in its own workspace. The old /f/employee_onboarding link, now shared, answered "ambiguous" instead of choosing. The public API, given A's workspace, filed into A despite B's higher version. A ticket from A's form was refused on B's (bad_ticket). A's draft token used on B's form started a new draft and left A's reading "Draft In A"; read through B's form it returned nothing. Publishing A again kept its link, and a key only A has still resolves by name.

proofs.name: The operator asks what is overdue and sends a reminder that matches what they confirmed
proofs.claim: Section 20.1 step 9, and 7.1: a permission-filtered query service with no raw model database access.
proofs.detail: "Which records are overdue" matched 3 of 3, every one past the SLA its state declares. A plan naming a state that does not exist was refused by the compiler (QRY002), and so was filtering on a restricted answer (QRY004) — which would have read restricted data one yes/no at a time without ever displaying it. An admin of another workspace asked the identical question and saw 1 of their own records and 0 of these — the plan cannot name a tenant, so the scope comes from who is asking. The preview authorized 3 target(s) one at a time; a stale digest was refused ("the plan changed since it was previewed — look at it ag"), and so was spending somebody else's preview ("refused: operate — a plan is confirmed by the person wh"). The confirmed run sent 3, a replay sent 0, and every reminder is on its record's own history.

proofs.name: Every action traces back to the request that caused it, across the worker boundary
proofs.claim: Section 20.2 observability: traceable request, event, job, attempt and result identifiers.
proofs.detail: One submission produced 1 event(s), 1 job(s) and 3 action run(s), every one carrying "proof-request-0001" and 0 unattributed. The actions ran in a later drain that knew nothing about the submission — the link survived because the request id is stamped on the outbox row and read back when the job runs. A timer firing got an id of its own (req_c58197c24200…) rather than inheriting one, because a deadline is its own cause. The support view joined them into 2 step(s) with every attempt count present, and answered in a sentence: "Queued: 1 job scheduled and not yet run. If this does not clear, no worker is ru". Asking by request id found 1 record; an admin of another workspace asking the same id found 0.

proofs.name: An administrator exports the record with its history, and only then is it deleted
proofs.claim: Section 20.1 step 11, and 6.4: corrections append history; destructive overwriting of audit evidence is prohibited.
proofs.detail: The bundle carried 4 history entries for a finished record — submission, both decisions with the reasons given, and every task completion — plus 2 approval(s), 2 message(s) and 1 document(s). An approver could not export at all ("neither the roles held (hiring_manager) nor workspace role "approver" grant "administer""). An administrator holding no process role saw every field; one who is also a hiring manager had 3 withheld (national_id, bank_account, right_to_work_reference) — named in the bundle rather than quietly absent, and not left in the answers as the literal string "[redacted]". The export is itself on the record's history, and a second export of an unchanged record produced the same checksum (d4842db14ad0), so a file can be verified later. Retention then deleted 1 instance and 7 event(s) — in that order, because afterwards there is nothing left to export.

proofs.name: A workspace can be created and joined, and nobody can grant more than they hold
proofs.claim: Section 6.1: IAM-01, IAM-04 and IAM-05 — three of the four Must rows that were not met.
proofs.detail: A workspace was created from nothing and its owner signed in; a five-character password was refused ("a password of at least 12 characters, pl"). Before confirming their own address they could not invite anybody ("confirm your own email address first — we sent y…"), because the invitation goes out under their name. The invitation showed the invitee the workspace name, their role and who asked — and nothing else — then created their account; the same link a second time was refused ("that invitation is not valid any more"). A builder holds "administer", so the capability check alone would have let them invite an owner and accept it themselves; they may grant builder, approver, analyst, read_only and were refused ("you hold "builder", which cannot grant "owner" — y"). Deactivating them revoked 1 live session and their token stopped resolving immediately. The only owner could neither deactivate nor demote themselves, because a workspace with no owner has nobody who can invite one. Accepting the invitation marked the new member's address verified, because following a link that was emailed to it is the proof a verification link asks for. An external identity resolved by subject, and still resolved after the email address changed — matching on the address is how one person ends up with two accounts.

proofs.name: Account recovery proves control of an address and cannot be used to find out who has one
proofs.claim: Section 12.1: verified email and password reset — the last two authentication rows.
proofs.detail: A verification link confirmed the address and was refused the second time ("that link is not valid any more — ask for a new one"). A link issued for one address did not verify a different one after the address changed ("that link was for a different address — ask …") — without that check, requesting a link and then editing your address verifies an address you never proved. A reset request for an address with an account and one without returned the same shape, and 0 messages went to the stranger. Spending the link revoked 1 live session, the old password stopped working, the new one worked, and the link was refused a second time. A deactivated member got no link at all — a reset would be the way back in for somebody an owner deliberately removed. Searching auth_token for either plaintext token found 0 rows: only the SHA-256 is stored, so a dump of that table is not a set of keys.

proofs.name: A second factor makes the password stop being enough, and cannot be replayed or guessed
proofs.claim: Section 12.1: the MFA option — the last unmet row in authentication.
proofs.detail: Before enrolment the password produced a session. Generating a secret did NOT turn the factor on — the password still worked — and a wrong code was refused ("that code is not right"); an enrolment that switches on when the secret is created locks out everybody whose scan silently failed. A real code confirmed it and returned 10 recovery codes. From then on the password returned a challenge instead of a session, and the challenge token resolved to nothing — it is not a session with a flag on it. Five wrong guesses were refused individually and the sixth was refused for exhausting the attempts; six digits is a million possibilities and unlimited guesses would make that number decorative. The code that confirmed enrolment could not then sign in ("that code has already been used — wait for the next one") — confirming spends that window like any other use. The next window's code signed in. That SAME code a moment later was refused ("that code has already been used — wait for the next one") while the next one worked — a code read over a shoulder is otherwise good for another thirty seconds. A phone two minutes fast still signed in, because rejecting clock drift is how a second factor becomes a support queue. A recovery code worked once and left 9; the same one again was refused. Searching for a plaintext recovery code found 0 rows. Turning it off with a valid authenticator code was refused ("that password is not right") — somebody holding the phone but not the password is exactly who must not remove the factor — and the password turned it off.

proofs.name: A bounce changes what the system does next, and a forged one changes nothing
proofs.claim: Section 6.6: the delivery log past `sent` — delivered, bounced, complained, and the suppression that follows.
proofs.detail: A signed notification verified; the same bytes with a different secret, one extra space, and an hour of age were each refused. A hard bounce moved the message to "bounced" and suppressed the address. The provider retries until it gets a 2xx, so the identical event was delivered again and was a no-op — 1 row, not two. A delivery notification arriving afterwards left the message "bounced": a message's state is the worst thing that happened to any recipient, and a later event never lowers it. A soft bounce suppressed nobody, because a full mailbox is not a dead one. An event for a message we never sent was recorded and matched nothing, rather than returning an error the provider would retry forever. Then the test that matters: the same address was mailed again by a second record and 0 messages left — the send was logged "skipped" reading "suppressed: bouncer@proof-delivery.test (hard_bounce)". An operator lifted it and a fresh hard bounce put it straight back, because the mail server gets the last word. A tenant that had never written to that address saw 0 suppressions while the tenant that had saw 1.

proofs.name: A privacy request erases one person without destroying anybody else
proofs.claim: Section 20.2 privacy: data map, deletion workflow. Section 12.1: privacy request workflow.
proofs.detail: The data map is derived from the published version: 20 fields, every restricted one carrying a reason and hidden from somebody, and it traces where a value goes — start_date reaches 12 destinations including a webhook that leaves the platform. A read_only member was refused it ("workspace role "read_only" does not grant "report""). The manager appears in 2 records and is the subject of none, so erasing them redacted 2 field(s) and deleted 0 records — both records survived and the address now reads "[erased]", so the audit still shows a manager was asked. A subject whose record is still running was left alone. An operator was refused ("workspace role "operator" does not grant "administer""). The preview reported 1 deletion and performed none. Erasing the finished record's subject removed it and all 4 of its events, and the erasure_run row records the same number — the account is written before the deletion and had to be counted first, or it would say zero.

proofs.name: A webhook actually leaves, is signed, survives a rotation, dies in a dead letter, and replays
proofs.claim: Section 11.2, against a real HTTP server that verifies the signature itself.
proofs.detail: A real server received 3 request(s) and verified every signature itself. The envelope carried the event, event id, instance id, process version and occurred-at that §11.2 names — before this, call_webhook wrote a row saying "delivered" and made no request at all. Registering a plain-http endpoint off localhost was refused ("a webhook endpoint must be https, except on localhost for development"). After rotating the secret the next delivery carried 2 signatures and the receiver, still using the old one, accepted it — which is what "rotate with overlap" is for. Against a failing endpoint the delivery retried to 6 attempts and stopped in a dead letter rather than retrying forever; it was inspectable, and replaying it once the endpoint recovered delivered it. An event with no subscriber left a "no_subscriber" row, because silence is indistinguishable from never having fired.

proofs.name: A worker fires deadlines with nobody watching
proofs.claim: Section 10.1: queue-backed workers. A deadline that needs an operator to open a page is not a deadline.
proofs.detail: Forty-nine hours passed with no request of any kind. The loop settled in 3 round(s), sent 1 reminder and left 0 due timers unfired.

proofs.name: Retention deletes, only for an administrator, and says what it removed
proofs.claim: Sections 9.2 and 12.1: configurable retention and deletion jobs, against an append-only history.
proofs.detail: An operator was refused ("neither the roles held (it_operator) nor workspace role "operator" grant "administer""). The preview reported 1 instance and 1 events and deleted nothing. The real run removed 1 instance and 1 events, leaving a retention_run row naming what went. The record still inside its retention period survived, and deleting its history outside the procedure is still refused.

proofs.name: Idempotent email under replay
proofs.claim: Section 6.5: a stable action key prevents duplicate emails, documents, webhooks, or charges.
proofs.detail: 1 email(s) after first delivery, 1 after two full replays. The outbox row was delivered 3 times; the action ran 3 time(s) and every replay short-circuited on the idempotency key.

proofs.name: Concurrent workers never double-process
proofs.claim: FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED gives each outbox row to exactly one worker, with no lock waits between them.
proofs.detail: 8 workers claimed 40 rows across 4 distinct worker ids; 40 emails for 40 instances (1 each), 0 duplicated effects.

proofs.name: A dead worker loses nothing and duplicates nothing
proofs.claim: A claimed row is invisible for its visibility timeout, then returns to the queue for someone else.
proofs.detail: Another worker saw 0 rows at +5s and 1 at +45s. The record reached "manager_review" with 1 email sent, not 2.

proofs.name: Timers fire once, on time, and are cancelled on exit
proofs.claim: Section 6.5: relative deadlines and reminders, stored canonically in UTC.
proofs.detail: Nothing at +47h, 1 firing at +49h, 0 on a second sweep at the same instant. 1 reminder sent; 1 pending timer cancelled when the record moved on.

proofs.name: A simulated clock moves only the tenant that invented it
proofs.claim: Section 9: the outbox is shared across tenants; a fabricated clock is not.
proofs.detail: Advancing my workspace fourteen days sent 1 reminder here and 0 next door. Their record's state clock is still in the past. An unscoped fabricated clock was refused.

proofs.name: Parallel work finishes in either order, and only when all of it is done
proofs.claim: docs/failure-cases.md G1: a fan-out modelled as a chain is slower than the real process and breaks if the work is done in the other order.
proofs.detail: Both tasks were open together (book_orientation, create_accounts, issue_equipment). Equipment first left the record in "provisioning"; accounts then took it to "complete". Accounts first left it in "provisioning"; equipment then took it to "complete". The join fired 1 time, on the completion that arrived last.

proofs.name: The person who submitted a record cannot approve it
proofs.claim: docs/failure-cases.md G5: the claimant types the approver address, so nothing stopped them typing their own.
proofs.detail: A £450 claim reached "manager_review", so there was a real decision to make. Approving their own claim was refused — "the person who submitted a record may not approve it" — and the record stayed in "manager_review". The same approval, named the same way, was decided by somebody else and the record moved to "approved".

proofs.name: A deadline can hang off a date in the record, and moves when that date does
proofs.claim: docs/failure-cases.md G4: the only clock was time-in-state, so a hire approved in March and one approved the day before they start got the same schedule.
proofs.detail: Two records entered provisioning at the same instant with start dates five months apart and got deadlines 2027-02-26 and 2026-10-02 — three days before each. The start date was moved to 16 November and the deadline followed to 2026-11-13. Draining twice past the date fired it 1 time and sent 1 chase, rather than looping on its own self-transition.

proofs.name: A double submission makes one case
proofs.claim: Section 4.2: duplicates are handled without losing the original audit trail.
proofs.detail: 1 instance from 2 concurrent submissions, 1 receipt sent. The second attempt is still on the record as "duplicate_submission_ignored".

proofs.name: A published version cannot be edited, and a live record keeps the version it started under
proofs.claim: Section 9.2: published versions are immutable; every instance records the version that governs it.
proofs.detail: Editing v1 was refused by the database, not by convention. Editing its event history was refused too. v2 is live, and the in-flight record still runs under v1.

proofs.name: Submission and workflow start are far inside the section 10.4 budget
proofs.claim: Beta targets: acknowledgment p95 under 1.5s, workflow start p95 under 30s.
proofs.detail: Over 100 submissions: acknowledgment p95 15.6ms (budget 1500ms), first action p95 39.5ms (budget 30000ms). Database round trips only, local container.
